content: Each time the content of the platform is updated, a new PDF version of the Guidelines will be made available for download on the WHO Global Malaria Programme website. This ensures accessibility in areas where internet connectivity is unavailable. However, users should be aware that downloaded PDFs may become outdated and may not reflect the most recent recommendations. Recommendations in this publication are based on advice from independent experts who have considered the best available evidence, risk-benefit analyses, and other relevant factors. For malaria prevention and control, pyrethroid-only long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) are strongly recommended for deployment in areas with ongoing malaria transmission. These nets are most effective where the primary malaria vectors bite predominantly at night. WHO recommends using prequalified insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) for protecting at-risk populations. Nets should be hung appropriately, avoiding direct sunlight, which can degrade insecticidal activity. In areas with pyrethroid resistance, pyrethroid-PBO ITNs may be deployed instead of pyrethroid-only LLINs. However, this recommendation is conditional due to the higher cost of pyrethroid-PBO ITNs and their uncertain cost-effectiveness. PBO is less wash-resistant than pyrethroids, leading to a faster decline in bioavailability over the three-year lifespan of an ITN. Evidence supporting this recommendation comes from limited studies in East Africa, and its applicability to other regions may vary. Pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs are recommended for deployment in areas with pyrethroid resistance, as they may provide greater protection. However, this recommendation is based on limited evidence from a single trial in Africa. Malaria programs should consider local vector characteristics and resistance mechanisms when deciding on the appropriateness of these nets. Pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs may be deployed in areas with pyrethroid resistance, but their use is conditional due to concerns about poor cost-effectiveness. This is attributed to their higher cost and the relatively short-lived additional impact compared to pyrethroid-only nets. WHO does not recommend deploying pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs over pyrethroid-PBO ITNs, as the latter are considered more cost-effective based on current data. Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) should also be deployed in humanitarian emergency settings to prevent and control malaria. The recommendation is limited to ITNs currently recommended by WHO. Infrastructure, access, logistical capacity, and resources must be considered when deploying ITNs in such settings. To achieve and maintain optimal ITN coverage, countries should combine mass free net distribution campaigns with other locally appropriate delivery mechanisms, such as antenatal care clinics and immunization programs. Recipients should be advised to continue using their nets, regardless of their condition or age, until replacement nets are available. Safe disposal of old nets and packaging materials should be ensured, preferably through high-temperature incineration or burial away from water sources. Indoor residual spraying (IRS) is recommended for malaria prevention and control in areas with ongoing transmission. Products from insecticide classes prequalified by WHO should be selected based on the susceptibility of local malaria vectors. IRS is appropriate where the majority of vectors feed and rest indoors, people sleep indoors at night, and the transmission pattern allows for protection with one or two rounds of spraying per year. In humanitarian emergency settings, IRS may be deployed, but its use is conditional due to very low certainty of evidence and concerns about feasibility and cost.
